section.title: The Glory Departs the Temple
section.sectionRationale: Ezekiel's inaugural throne vision by the River Kebar reappears inside the temple itself, but only to leave it. Having exposed the idolatry hidden within the house that bears His Name, God's glory rises from the Most Holy Place, pauses at the threshold, and moves at last to the east gate, a slow, visible withdrawal that proves no building, however sacred, can hold a God whose people no longer want Him.
section.thesis: Because Jerusalem's temple has been filled with idols, the glory of the LORD deliberately withdraws stage by stage, from above the cherubim to the threshold to the east gate, showing that God's presence was never a fixture of the building but a Person who can, and does, leave; yet this same glory is promised to return, a hope realized when the Word became flesh and tabernacled among us.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the man in linen sent among the cherubim to scatter burning coals of judgment over the city; a detailed vision of the cherubim and their wheels, the same living creatures Ezekiel saw by the Kebar, now named; and the glory's unhurried departure, first above the cherubim, then to the threshold, then out to the east gate of the LORD's house.

units.label: Coals for the city
units.note: judgment scattered from among the cherubim

verses.text: And I looked and saw above the expanse, above the heads of the cherubim, the likeness of a throne of sapphire.

And the LORD said to the man clothed in linen, “Go inside the {{galgal|wheelwork}} beneath the cherubim. Fill your hands with burning coals from among the cherubim and scatter them over the city.” And as I watched, he went in.
Now when the man went in, the cherubim were standing on the south side of the temple, and a cloud filled the inner court.

Then the {{kavod|glory}} of the LORD rose from above the cherubim and stood over the threshold of the temple. The temple was filled with the cloud, and the court was filled with the brightness of the glory of the LORD.
The sound of the wings of the cherubim could be heard as far as the outer court, like the voice of God Almighty when He speaks.
When the LORD commanded the man clothed in linen, saying, “Take fire from within the wheelwork, from among the cherubim,” the man went in and stood beside a wheel.
Then one of the cherubim reached out his hand and took some of the fire that was among them. And he put it into the hands of the man clothed in linen, who received it and went out.

units.label: The cherubim and their wheels
units.note: the living creatures from the Kebar, named at last

verses.text: (The cherubim appeared to have the form of human hands under their wings.)
Then I looked and saw four wheels beside the cherubim, one wheel beside each {{keruv|cherub}}. And the wheels gleamed like a beryl stone.
As for their appearance, all four had the same form, like a wheel within a wheel.
When they moved, they would go in any of the four directions, without turning as they moved. For wherever the head faced, the cherubim would go in that direction, without turning as they moved.
Their entire bodies, including their backs, hands, and wings, were full of eyes all around, as were their four wheels.
I heard the wheels being called “the whirling {{galgal|wheels}}.”
Each of the cherubim had four faces: the first face was that of a cherub, the second that of a man, the third that of a lion, and the fourth that of an eagle.
Then the cherubim rose upward. These were the living creatures I had seen by the River Kebar.
When the cherubim moved, the wheels moved beside them, and even when they spread their wings to rise from the ground, the wheels did not veer away from their side.
When the cherubim stood still, the wheels also stood still, and when they ascended, the wheels ascended with them, for the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels.

units.label: The glory departs
units.note: from the Most Holy Place to the threshold to the east gate

verses.text: Then the glory of the LORD moved away from the threshold of the temple and stood above the cherubim.

As I watched, the cherubim lifted their wings and rose up from the ground, with the wheels beside them as they went. And they stopped at the entrance of the east gate of the house of the LORD, with the glory of the God of Israel above them.
These were the living creatures I had seen beneath the God of Israel by the River Kebar, and I knew that they were cherubim.
Each had four faces and four wings, with what looked like human hands under their wings.
Their faces looked like the faces I had seen by the River Kebar. Each creature went straight ahead.

kavod.gloss: Glory, weightiness. The kavod of the LORD is the visible, weighty manifestation of His presence that filled the tabernacle and temple. It is a Person, not a fixture, who can rise, move, and depart when His holiness meets unrepentant idolatry.

keruv.gloss: Cherub, a class of guardian heavenly being. Ezekiel here names the four living creatures of his inaugural vision, chapter 1, as cherubim, the same order of being that guarded Eden's entrance after the fall, Genesis 3:24, and whose images overshadowed the ark's mercy seat.

galgal.gloss: Wheel, a whirling thing. Verse 13 names the wheels 'the whirling wheels', galgal, conveying restless, rapid mobility. God's throne chariot is never static or confined to one location; it can move wherever His purposes take it, even away from a defiled temple.

basic.context: Fourteen months after his inaugural vision, Ezekiel sees the same throne chariot again, but this time inside the temple itself, and he watches its terrible business: judgment coals scattered over Jerusalem, and then, in slow, deliberate stages, the glory of the LORD rising up and moving out. The building the people trusted as their guarantee of safety is being abandoned by the very presence that made it holy.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real visionary experience given to a real prophet in dated, historical circumstances, not merely a symbol invented for effect. The hardest, plainest truth is that God's presence in a sacred place is never an automatic possession; when a people persist in defiling His house, He can, and does, withdraw, even from His own temple.
basic.originalLanguages: The kavod, the glory, is a weighty, visible Person, not a fixture bolted to the building. The keruvim, cherubim, are named here as the same living creatures from Ezekiel's first vision, the same order of being that guarded Eden after the fall. Their wheels, galgal, whirl in every direction at once, showing that God's throne is never confined to a single place, not even the temple in Jerusalem.
basic.typology: The gradual departure of the glory, first from the Most Holy Place, then to the threshold, then to the east gate, anticipates its promised return in Ezekiel 43, and finds its greater fulfillment when the Word became flesh and tabernacled among us, John 1:14, and when, at the cross, the temple veil was torn, showing that the old order was giving way to a new and better dwelling of God with His people.
basic.christ: The glory that reluctantly leaves the temple in this vision is the same glory that comes to dwell permanently in Christ, who is Himself the true temple, John 2:19-21. Jesus wept over Jerusalem and foretold the temple's ruin, Matthew 23:37 to 24:2, standing in the line of Ezekiel's warning; but what Ezekiel watched depart in judgment, the Gospels show returning in mercy, and Revelation shows never departing again, for 'the dwelling place of God is with man', Revelation 21:3.
basic.god: God is holy, so much so that He will not remain among unrepented idolatry even in His own house; yet He is also patient and precise, moving in visible, unhurried stages rather than vanishing at once, giving every possible last witness to the city before the end comes.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Kings 8:10-11 records the glory first filling Solomon's temple. Ezekiel 1:4-28 is the same throne chariot vision by the Kebar. Ezekiel 43:1-5 promises the glory's return to a future temple. John 1:14 shows the Word tabernacling among us. Revelation 21:3 and 22 promise God's dwelling with man forever, with no need of a temple, for the Lamb is its temple.
basic.oneStory: This is the moment the temple's whole claim to safety collapses: the glory that made the building holy chooses to leave it. But the glory that departed in judgment is promised to return, and returns for good in Jesus Christ, God tabernacling permanently among His people, until the day there is no temple left to leave, only the unshielded presence of God with His people forever.

context.literary:
Chapter 10 is built from two interleaved strands, and a good way into it is to follow them separately. The first strand is the errand of the man in linen, who is sent in 10:2 and returns by 10:7 with his hands full of fire. The second is the description of the cherubim and their wheels, 10:8 to 17, which interrupts the errand and makes no progress in the plot. Then the plot resumes in 10:18, when the glory leaves. The pause is deliberate. Ezekiel is slowing the scene to let the reader see what exactly is leaving, and the long description is also an argument: the throne that is departing is the very throne he saw by the Kebar, and the narrator says so twice, 10:15 and 10:20.

The chapter is also the second of four stations in a single exit. The glory leaves the Most Holy Place for the threshold in 9:3, stands over the threshold in 10:4, moves out to the east gate in 10:18 and 19, and finally rises from the city to the mountain on the east in 11:23. Each step is announced with a short verb of rising or standing, and each step is separated from the next by something the prophet is shown. The effect is a withdrawal that is slow enough to be a last offer.

The chapter is a deliberate retelling of Ezekiel 1, with changes. The throne is sapphire again, 10:1 and 1:26. The creatures are the same, 10:15 and 10:20. But the setting is now inside the temple court and the tone is now judgment. The vision that once opened the heavens over exiles now closes over the house they remembered.
context.historical:
For a priest like Ezekiel, the cherubim were not strange creatures. Two olive wood cherubim, each ten cubits high, stood in the inner sanctuary of Solomon's temple, 1 Kings 6:23 to 28, and the ark beneath them was spoken of as the throne from which the LORD ruled: 'He is enthroned above the cherubim,' Psalm 99:1, and 'who sits enthroned between the cherubim,' 1 Samuel 4:4. Ezekiel's vision takes that furniture and sets it in motion. The throne has wheels. The place of the Presence is not a fixed object but a chariot that can go where its Lord goes. Nothing in the chapter mentions the ark, and the vision makes no attempt to save it.

That was a heavy thing to say to a people who had a long habit of trusting the temple. The memory of Solomon's dedication, when the cloud filled the house and the priests could not stand to minister, 1 Kings 8:10 and 11, had given Jerusalem a settled belief that God had come to stay. Ezekiel shows the cloud filling the court again, 10:3 and 10:4, but this time it is a cloud of leaving. Shiloh offered a precedent that Jeremiah had pressed on his hearers, 'He abandoned the tabernacle of Shiloh,' Psalm 78:60, and when the ark was taken in Eli's day the cry had gone up that the glory had departed, 1 Samuel 4:21 and 22.

The date is some five or six years before the city's fall. For Ezekiel's exiles, the practical meaning was sobering: the temple in Jerusalem, which they were longing to return to, was already empty of the Presence. The next chapter shows that God was not absent from them but present in exile, and that the real homeland of His glory was not a place on a map.
context.canonical:
The chapter is deeply dependent on earlier Scripture and heavily used by later Scripture. Its throne of sapphire comes from the elders' vision on Sinai, where under God's feet was something like a pavement of sapphire, Exodus 24:10. The cloud filling a sanctuary recalls the tabernacle, Exodus 40:34 and 35, and Solomon's temple, 2 Chronicles 7:1 to 3. The cherubim carry the memory of Eden, Genesis 3:24, and of the mercy seat, Exodus 25:18 to 22. The picture of God riding on a cherub is older still, in David's song, 'He mounted a cherub and flew,' Psalm 18:10.

The chapter prepares an answer further on. Ezekiel 43:1 to 5 records the glory returning from the east by the very gate through which it left, and says that the vision was 'like the visions I had seen by the River Kebar.' Ezekiel 44:2 adds that the east gate is to stay shut because the LORD entered it.

In the New Testament the vision is read through Jesus. John tells us the Word 'made His dwelling among us' and that we saw His glory, John 1:14, and says Isaiah saw Jesus' glory, John 12:41. Jesus pronounces the house left desolate, Matthew 23:38, and speaks of the temple of His body, John 2:19 to 21. The Spirit is then poured out as fire resting on each believer, Acts 2:3, and Paul calls the church a dwelling for God in the Spirit, Ephesians 2:21 and 22. The end of the Bible makes the vision into a promise: the glory of God lights the city, and there is no temple in it, Revelation 21:22 and 23.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel wrote for people who believed in the temple the way people believe in a fortress. His aim was to break that belief without breaking their faith in God. To do this he had to show them something that was impossible to imagine, the glory leaving, and he had to do it with such care that they could not suspect it was a metaphor for something smaller. The slow stages, the wheels, the eyes and the cherubim are all there to say that the one who left was the God of the whole cosmos, who could not be forced to remain.

There is a second purpose that sits behind the first. By describing the throne he had seen at the Kebar, in the exile, Ezekiel told the exiles that the God who departed Jerusalem had already come to them. Their situation, which they took as abandonment, was nearer to presence than the situation of the people at home. The chapter is a verdict on the temple, but a comfort to the exiles, and the author wants both heard.

He also wants the people to take responsibility without despair. The glory does not leave suddenly or in anger alone. It moves in stages that give every chance for the people to turn, and the preceding chapters have shown that they were not turning. The chapter wants to make plain that leaving was the last, reluctant act of a God who had stayed through years of provocation, and that its cause lay in the abominations of chapter 8, not in any weakness of His own.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter reports a vision of what God did to a particular temple in a particular generation. It does not say that He abandons every house or every people at the first failure, and it should not be applied as a threat to believers who have fallen. The New Testament, in fact, is very clear that those who are in Christ are not abandoned, Hebrews 13:5, and that the Spirit is given as a seal and a pledge, 2 Corinthians 1:22.

What it does prescribe, by example, is a posture towards holy things. Sacred space, sacred offices and sacred practice do not secure God's presence. Presence is the gift of a God who dwells among those who honour Him, and the church is now His temple, 1 Corinthians 3:16 and 17. Paul's warning there, that God will destroy anyone who destroys His temple, carries the Ezekiel pattern forward. Practical application follows: communities are to take care over what they allow in their gatherings, and individuals over what they bring into the body that houses the Spirit. At the same time, the chapter should be read gently by anyone afraid that they have driven God away. The visions of Ezekiel 11 and 36 follow the departure with promises of a heart renewed and a Spirit given.

debates.question: Why does the first face of the cherub in 10:14 differ from the face described in Ezekiel 1:10?

views.label: A scribal or editorial accident
views.case: In 1:10 the four faces are man, lion, ox and eagle. In 10:14 the list is cherub, man, lion and eagle, and the ox is missing. Some scholars think an early copyist introduced the difference, or that the text of one chapter was tidied. The weakness of this view is that there is no manuscript evidence that settles it and the verse reads smoothly as it stands.

views.label: A deliberate identification
views.case: Ezekiel has just said in 10:15 and 10:20 that these are the living creatures he saw at the Kebar and that he now knew they were cherubim. The change of face may be a way of saying that the ox of the earlier vision belongs to the same order of beings as the cherub, so that the creatures he saw in exile are the cherubim of the temple. On this view the variation is part of the point.

views.label: A change of perspective
views.case: Some see in the shift a difference of viewing angle or role: in chapter 1 the creatures serve the throne in heaven, in chapter 10 they serve the throne in the temple. The first face being called cherub marks the face turned toward the earth in the temple context.

debates.bearing: Nothing in the theology depends on the answer, and the safest course is to admit that we do not know. What is clear is the statement of 10:20, that the creatures in the temple are those at the Kebar, which is the point the author wanted heard.

debates.question: Is the departure of the glory final, or only a pause before judgment?

views.label: A final withdrawal until the future temple
views.case: The glory leaves in four stages and does not return in the book until 43:1 to 5, many years later in the prophet's timeline and after the city has fallen. On this reading, the second temple never saw the glory as the first had, and the return awaits a future temple or a greater fulfilment.

views.label: A withdrawal with the exiles in view
views.case: 11:16 says that God has been a sanctuary for the exiles in the countries where they went, and the throne chariot is itself the vehicle of a God who is on the move. The departure is therefore also a journey toward the exiles, and the same glory that left appears among them by the Kebar in chapters 1 and 3.

views.label: A judgment that carries a promise
views.case: The glory stands at the east gate and then on the mountain east of the city, 10:19 and 11:23, as if it were waiting. The east is also the direction from which it will come back, 43:2. On this reading even the departure is staged in a way that leaves room for the return.

debates.bearing: The three views are not rivals. The chapter records a real withdrawal, with real consequences for the temple, and the rest of Ezekiel shows that the withdrawal was the beginning of a larger movement of God toward His scattered people.

study.originalLanguages:
Four features of the Hebrew help explain why this chapter is so strange and why its first hearers could not have missed its meaning.

The first is the word that the BSB translates 'wheelwork,' 'wheel' and 'whirling wheels.' Ezekiel 1:15 uses the word ophan for the wheels, and Ezekiel 10:9 begins with the same word. But in 10:2, 10:6 and 10:13 the term is galgal, which has the sense of something that rolls, or turns over. Verse 13 is peculiar: 'I heard the wheels being called' galgal, as though a voice in the vision gave them the name. The word is related to the Aramaic that Daniel uses for the throne of the Ancient of Days, whose 'wheels were all ablaze,' Daniel 7:9. The point is that the throne of God is a thing of motion and fire, not a piece of fixed furniture.

The second is the verb for what the man in linen does with the coals. He is told to scatter them over the city. The verb is zaraq, which is the verb for tossing or dashing, used for the sprinkling of blood against the altar, Leviticus 1:5, and for Moses flinging soot toward the sky as a plague, Exodus 9:8. The coals are being thrown from the sanctuary toward the city in the same gesture by which priests applied what was holy. It is a priestly act turned into judgment. The burning coals themselves were part of the first vision, 1:13, and the cherub places them in the linen man's hands, 10:7, so that even the instrument of the burning comes from the throne.

The third is the word for the glory, kavod, which has the root sense of weight. When the glory stands over the threshold, 10:4, and the cloud fills the court, the vocabulary is almost the same as that used when Solomon's temple was filled, 1 Kings 8:10 and 11. The sound of the cherubim's wings is described as 'the voice of God Almighty,' 10:5, and the BSB footnote records that the Hebrew has El-Shaddai, the old name of patriarchal promise. It is the name that was chosen to be used here, at a moment when a promise-keeping God is withdrawing his dwelling.

The fourth is the cluster of verbs of motion. The glory 'rose,' 'stood,' 'moved away' and 'stopped,' 10:4, 10:18 and 10:19. Numbers 9:17 uses the same range for the cloud that governed Israel's journeys: when it was lifted the people set out, and where it settled they camped. Ezekiel's glory is moving in the same manner as the guiding cloud of the wilderness, but its camp has become the east gate. The last detail is the sentence that the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels, 10:17. The word is ruach, the same word for spirit, wind and breath, and it explains why the wheels move without turning: one will governs the whole chariot.

typology.type: The glory leaving the house, Ezekiel 10:18 and 19
typology.fulfillment: The glory withdraws from Solomon's temple in stages, and its departure leaves the house empty of what made it holy. Jesus repeats the verdict when He says to Jerusalem, 'Look, your house is left to you desolate,' Matthew 23:38, and the veil is torn from top to bottom at His death, Matthew 27:51. The correspondence is of a house that has lost its Presence. The escalation is that the Presence does not now go away from people but into them: the Word 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, and then the Spirit fills His people, Acts 2:3 and 4. The type falls short because Ezekiel's glory leaves a place, while Christ's glory comes to persons.

typology.type: The east gate as the way out and the way back, Ezekiel 10:19
typology.fulfillment: The glory stops at the east gate, and Ezekiel later sees it coming in by that gate, 43:1 to 4. Jesus comes down from the Mount of Olives to the city on a donkey as the king who comes in the name of the Lord, Luke 19:37 and 38, and He ascends from the same mountain, Acts 1:9 to 12, with the promise that He will return in the same way. Zechariah 14:4 sets His feet on that mountain. The correspondence is geographical and real, and the type is not yet finished, since the return in glory is still to come.

typology.type: The coals from between the cherubim, Ezekiel 10:2 and 7
typology.fulfillment: Fire from the throne is carried to Jerusalem to burn it. Isaiah's coal from the altar, carried by a seraph, touched his lips and took away his guilt, Isaiah 6:6 and 7, so that the same fire can purge or consume. In Revelation an angel fills a censer with fire from the altar and hurls it to the earth, Revelation 8:5. At Pentecost the fire comes as tongues resting on each believer, Acts 2:3. The type shows that the fire of God's holiness is never neutral. In Christ it becomes the fire of cleansing and of the Spirit for those who are His, and the fire of judgment for those who refuse Him.

typology.type: The throne that moves, Ezekiel 10:9 to 17
typology.fulfillment: A throne on wheels with creatures full of eyes announces that God is not tied to Jerusalem. Stephen quotes Isaiah to say that the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands, Acts 7:48 and 49. The throne of Revelation 4 and 5 is encircled by living creatures covered with eyes, and the Lamb is in the center of it, Revelation 5:6. The correspondence is of a throne that sees and goes everywhere. The escalation is that the one who sits at its centre is the Lamb who was slain, so the God who cannot be contained has also come close.

study.christ:
This chapter moves toward Christ along the line of the glory itself. The Hebrew Scriptures speak of the glory of the LORD as His visible presence, the weight and radiance of who He is. The New Testament says that this glory has a face. John writes, 'We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father,' John 1:14, and adds that Isaiah, when he saw the LORD high and lifted up, 'saw Jesus' glory,' John 12:41. Hebrews says the Son is 'the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature,' Hebrews 1:3. Ezekiel's glory, with its figure like a man on a throne of sapphire, 1:26, is therefore not a separate thing from the one who came in the flesh.

Because of this, the departure of the glory is one half of a great exchange. In Ezekiel, the glory leaves a house that has defiled it. In the Gospels, the glory enters history in a person and is found among people the temple authorities counted unclean. Jesus is called Emmanuel, God with us, and the glory that left by the east gate comes down the Mount of Olives toward the city, Luke 19:37 to 41. At that same moment He weeps, and He says the house is left desolate, Matthew 23:37 to 39. He knows what Ezekiel saw. He also says to the temple authorities, 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again,' and John explains that He spoke of the temple of His body, John 2:19 to 21. The body of Jesus is the place where the glory now lives, and so the old house can be left.

The way back is through His death. The veil of the temple, which marked the place where the cherubim were woven and the glory was thought to sit, was torn from top to bottom, Matthew 27:51, and Hebrews says that we may now enter by a new and living way through His body, Hebrews 10:19 and 20. The glory that Ezekiel saw lifting from the threshold has been brought back to humanity in Jesus and is not to be driven away again.

The pattern continues in the church. Jesus promised that the Father and He would come to anyone who loves Him and make a home with that person, John 14:23, and the Spirit was poured out after His exaltation, Acts 2:33. Paul can therefore say that believers are being built together into a dwelling place for God in His Spirit, Ephesians 2:22.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Not every cherub and wheel is a code for Christ, and the New Testament does not treat them that way. The vision is about a historical withdrawal from a historical house. But the New Testament does take its central claim, that the glory of God can come and go from a house and that it is a person, and answers it with the one in whom the glory has taken up permanent residence.
study.god:
Ezekiel 10 gives a picture of God that is hard to hold without strain, and it is helpful to name the pieces.

He is transcendent. The throne is above the expanse and above the heads of the cherubim, 10:1, and the creatures that carry it are covered in eyes, 10:12, and move with a single spirit, 10:17. He is not defined by any building. The theology that said God was in the temple the way a man is in his house was wrong from the beginning, as Solomon had admitted in his prayer: 'Will God indeed dwell upon the earth? Even heaven, the highest heaven, cannot contain You, much less this temple I have built,' 1 Kings 8:27. The wheels say the same thing in the language of vision.

He is also immanent, and this is the surprising half. The same God who is above the cherubim stands over the threshold, 10:4, and fills the court with the brightness of His glory. He enters the temple by covenant and by choice. His leaving is therefore not the removal of a force but the withdrawal of a person, and it is done reluctantly, in stages, with a pause at each gate. The word for the glory means weight, and the weight is being lifted from a place that had been entrusted with it.

He is holy and just. The fire taken from between the cherubim is the instrument of judgment, and it is scattered over a city that has filled the land with violence, 9:9. It is also true that the fire comes from the same place where mercy was sprinkled on the mercy seat. The cherubim are those of the mercy seat, Exodus 25:18 to 22, and the God who promised to meet His people there is the God who now sends fire from beneath them. Justice and mercy are not in different places in God. They are the same holiness, meeting people in different relationships.

He is faithful in the way He judges. The departure is slow, and this slowness is mercy. It gives the city a last chance to repent, and it makes it plain that the people could not blame a sudden change in God. The abominations were already there, and He had borne them long. His patience is not the weakness of an absent God, and His leaving is not the temper of an angry one.

He also holds to His purposes beyond His departure. The glory that is carried out on the chariot of the cherubim comes back in 43:1 to 5, in a vision Ezekiel says is like the one at the Kebar. The God who leaves is the God who has not finished.

For worship, the chapter calls for awe and for sobriety. We are asked to approach a God who sees with a thousand eyes, who cannot be managed by ritual, and who cannot be held in a house. We are also asked to be grateful that, in Christ, this same glory has made its home among us and has not been taken away.

crossReferences.note: The first vision, which Ezekiel says in 10:15 and 10:20 is the same as this one. Setting them side by side shows the same throne, the same creatures and the same likeness of glory. In chapter 1 they come to exiles with a commission. In chapter 10 they leave a temple with a sentence.

The elders of Israel at Sinai saw the God of Israel with a pavement of sapphire under His feet. Ezekiel's throne of sapphire in 10:1 draws on that scene, so that the God who gave the law at Sinai is the same God who now judges those who broke it.

When Solomon's temple was dedicated, the cloud filled the house and the priests could not minister because of the glory. Ezekiel's cloud in 10:3 and 4 uses the same language in reverse: the filling that once celebrated the arrival now accompanies the departure.

After the ark was captured, Eli's daughter in law named her son Ichabod and said the glory had departed from Israel. Ezekiel sees a far deeper departure, one that is not caused by Philistine hands but by the people's own abominations, and it takes place with the ark and its throne still in place.

David sings that God mounted a cherub and flew. Ezekiel's cherubim with their wheels are the Old Testament's fullest picture of what that flight looked like, and the psalm shows that the chariot of God was never merely a vision for exiles but a long established part of Israel's worship.

The reversal of chapter 10. The glory comes back from the east, by the gate through which it left, and fills the temple as it had filled it before. The prophet says the vision is like the one at the Kebar and like the one when God came to destroy the city. The two chapters are meant to be read together.

A seraph takes a burning coal from the altar and touches Isaiah's lips, and his guilt is taken away. In Ezekiel 10:2 and 7 a cherub gives burning coals to be scattered over a city. The same fire from the same throne room cleanses a repentant man and consumes an unrepentant city.

The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us, and His glory was seen. The Greek verb for dwelling recalls the tabernacle. What left Jerusalem in Ezekiel's vision comes back in a person, with grace and truth, and the departure is answered by arrival.

Jesus laments over Jerusalem and says, 'Look, your house is left to you desolate.' He speaks as someone who knows the history of Ezekiel 10 and sees it threatening to repeat, and He adds the promise that they will see Him again when they say, 'Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.'

Stephen quotes Isaiah to say that the Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands. It is the same truth the wheels of Ezekiel teach, and it was the reason that the Jewish leaders were so angry: they had made the temple into something it was never meant to be.

John sees no temple in the new city, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple, and the glory of God lights it. Ezekiel's departing glory is fully answered here: the glory no longer rises from a house, because it has become the light in which God's people live.

study.oneStory:
Scripture begins with God dwelling with His creatures and ends with His dwelling among them again, and in between the story is repeatedly one of presence granted, presence abused and presence withdrawn. In Eden, God walked in the garden in the breeze of the day, and after the fall cherubim were set at the east, Genesis 3:8 and 3:24. In the wilderness the glory filled the tabernacle and guided the camp, Exodus 40:34 to 38, and in the land it filled Solomon's temple, 1 Kings 8:10 and 11. The story that Ezekiel 10 tells is the sad second movement of this long pattern: a people given the greatest gift of God's nearness who treated it as a possession.

The chapter is, in a way, the first Eden story told again with the roles reversed. At the beginning, humanity was driven out of the garden while the cherubim were stationed to guard its entrance. Here the cherubim themselves rise and leave, and the glory goes with them, so that the sanctuary is left to those who had defiled it. The east, in the Bible's geography, is the direction of exile, and the glory takes up its station there. The exile of the people from the land is preceded by the exile of the glory from the house.

The story does not stop here. The prophets after Ezekiel look for a return, and the book itself ends with a city named 'The LORD is there,' Ezekiel 48:35. The return begins in Jesus. The glory comes again to Jerusalem from the east side, over the Mount of Olives, and is met by a city that does not know the time of its visitation, Luke 19:41 to 44. He enacts in his body what Ezekiel described in the building: the temple is destroyed and raised, John 2:19 to 21. After His ascension He sends the Spirit, and the dwelling place of God is no longer a house but a people, built together in Him, Ephesians 2:21 and 22.

The end of the story gathers every thread. John sees no temple in the new Jerusalem, because God and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22. There is no east gate for the glory to leave by, because there is no more curse and no more night, and the glory of God lights the city, Revelation 21:23 and 22:3 to 5. The God who was borne out of a defiled house on a chariot of fire is, at the last, the God who is borne into the midst of His people and does not go away. The chapter's grief is answered by the great voice from the throne: 'the dwelling place of God is with man,' Revelation 21:3.

sermon.title: Does God Ever Give Up on People? (Ezek. 10-11)
sermon.why: Carson works through Ezekiel 10 and 11 together, tracing the glory's departure from the temple and showing how, even in this scene of God seemingly giving people over to their sin, hope breaks through, exactly the tension this study holds between righteous withdrawal and future promise.

quiz.q: What does the man clothed in linen do with coals taken from among the cherubim?

options.text: He scatters them over the city as an act of judgment, Ezekiel 10:2.
options.note: Verse 2 explicitly commands the coals to be scattered over Jerusalem.

options.text: He offers them on the altar as incense.
options.note: The coals evoke sacrificial fire, but here they are scattered as judgment, not offered as incense.

options.text: He carries them to Ezekiel as a sign of comfort.
options.note: The coals are not brought to Ezekiel; they are scattered over the doomed city.

options.text: He extinguishes them to prevent the city's destruction.
options.note: The coals are used to bring judgment, not to prevent it.

quiz.q: In what stages does the glory of the LORD move in this chapter?

options.text: From above the cherubim in the Most Holy Place, to the threshold, and finally to the east gate.
options.note: Verses 4, 18-19 trace this exact, deliberate sequence.

options.text: It never actually leaves the temple in this chapter.
options.note: The chapter records real, visible movement out toward the east gate.

options.text: It moves only as far as the outer court and stays there permanently.
options.note: By the chapter's end the glory has reached the east gate, further than the outer court.

options.text: It vanishes instantly the moment the coals are scattered.
options.note: The departure is described as gradual and staged, not instantaneous.

quiz.q: How does Ezekiel identify the four living creatures in this chapter?

options.text: As cherubim, the same living creatures he saw in his inaugural vision by the River Kebar.
options.note: Verses 15 and 20 state plainly these are the same creatures, now named cherubim.

options.text: As ordinary temple guards dressed for battle.
options.note: These are heavenly beings, not human guards.

options.text: As idols the people had set up in the temple.
options.note: The cherubim belong to God's own throne vision; the idols are what provoked the glory's departure, not the cherubim themselves.

options.text: As angels sent for the first time to judge Jerusalem.
options.note: They are heavenly beings involved in judgment, but Ezekiel is explicit they are not new; he had already seen them by the Kebar.

quiz.q: What does the detail of eyes covering the cherubim and their wheels emphasize?

options.text: God's complete, all-seeing knowledge; nothing in the temple's corruption escapes His sight.
options.note: Verse 12 describes eyes covering their bodies and wheels, picturing total divine awareness.

options.text: That the wheels are decorated for ceremonial beauty.
options.note: The eyes are not decorative; they convey the vision's theological weight of divine sight.

options.text: That the cherubim are simply strange or frightening in appearance.
options.note: The strangeness is real, but the detail specifically serves the theme of God's unlimited sight.

options.text: That the vision has no theological significance, only artistic detail.
options.note: Every detail in Ezekiel's visions carries theological freight; this one underscores God's omniscience.

quiz.q: What is the ultimate significance of the glory's departure from the temple?

options.text: It shows God's presence is never automatic; He will not dwell where holiness is defied, though this glory is promised to return and finally dwell with His people through Christ.
options.note: The chapter's movement anticipates Ezekiel 43 and its fulfillment in John 1:14 and Revelation 21.

options.text: It is simply a literary flourish with no bearing on Israel's actual history.
options.note: The vision is tied to real, dated historical circumstances and the coming fall of Jerusalem.

options.text: It shows that God abandoned Israel forever with no hope of restoration.
options.note: The wider book of Ezekiel, including chapter 11's promise of a new heart, insists this withdrawal is not final abandonment.

options.text: It proves that the temple was never truly holy to begin with.
options.note: The temple was genuinely filled with the glory at its dedication, 1 Kings 8; its holiness is precisely what makes the later departure so grave.

questions: The glory left the temple only after the people filled it with idols. What might you be allowing into your own heart, the true temple of the Spirit, that grieves God's presence there?
God's departure was slow and visible, not sudden, as though giving every last chance to see and repent. Where might God be patiently warning you right now before a harder discipline comes?
The exiles could easily have felt abandoned when the glory departed. When you feel God distant, how does Ezekiel 11:19's promise of a new heart shape your hope even in seasons that feel like exile?
The temple's whole claim to safety collapsed when God's presence left it. What buildings, routines, or religious habits are you leaning on for security instead of a living relationship with God?
Christ is the true temple in whom the glory of God dwells permanently. How does knowing that God's presence in Him will never depart change the way you approach seasons of doubt or spiritual dryness?

translationNotes.note: The word rendered 'wheelwork' describes the mobile chariot-like structure beneath the cherubim; the BSB keeps a somewhat mechanical term to convey the strange, engineered quality of the vision rather than a smooth, simple wheel.

The wheels are given a name, 'the whirling wheels', which some translations render 'galgal' as a proper designation, underscoring that Ezekiel is recounting a term he specifically heard used for this feature of the vision.

Where Ezekiel 1:10 lists an ox as one of the four faces, this verse lists a cherub; most interpreters take this as the same vision described from a angle now that the creatures have been formally identified as cherubim, rather than a contradiction.
